newsitem.title: USA: New archbishop greeted warmly by Chicago.
newsitem.headline: New archbishop greeted warmly by Chicago.

text.p: The surprise appointment of Bishop Francis George to head the second-largest Roman Catholic community in the United States won widespread approval on Tuesday, though some liberals said they would wait to see how open he would be to dissent.

The 60-year-old George, who grew up in a gritty blue-collar Chicago neighbourhood where he was struck by polio as a youngster, will become the eighth archbishop of Chicago on May 7, the first native of the city to hold the post.

Asked at a news conference if he would try to work for common ground between liberal and conservative factions within the church, as did his widely admired predecessor, Cardinal Joseph Bernardin, George said:

"The faith isn't liberal or conservative. The faith is true. And so I'll preach the faith as Cardinal Bernardin preached and taught it. There's no difference in substance. He gave his life for the faith and for the church and I'll do the same."

George, a member of the poor-care Oblates of Mary Immaculate order, has been bishop of Portland, Oregon, for 10 months and was bishop of Yakima, Washington, before that. His name had not surfaced in speculation about the Chicago post since Bernardin died of cancer at age 68 in November 1996.

The Rev. Andrew Greeley, novelist and sociologist whose research often has uncovered wide diffences between what Rome preaches and what U.S. Catholics believe on matters such as birth control and role of women in the church, called George "very articulate and very charming."

"The question remains how open is he going to be to what's going on in the church ... he says he's going to preach the faith. Is birth control part of the faith when at least 85 percent dissent on that?" Greeley asked.
Church teaching prohibits artificial contraception. Pope John Paul has consistenty opposed the ordination of women.

Call to Action, a Chicago-based liberal group that advocates the priesthood for women, issued a conciliatory statement saying it hoped to have the same kind of "cordial and mutually respectful relationship" with George that it had with his predecessor.

Scott Appleby, director of the Cushaw Centre for the Study of American Catholicism at the University of Notre Dame, said George's order traditionally has been a strong supporter of papal infallability. "He is ready to dialogue," Appleby said, "but probably not on issues that are already defined by Rome."
